source: In behalf of the dignity of whaling, I would fain advance naught but substantiated facts. But after embattling his facts, an advocate who should wholly suppress a not unreasonable surmise, which might tell eloquently upon his cause—such an advocate, would he not be blameworthy?

It is well known that at the coronation of kings and queens, even modern ones, a certain curious process of seasoning them for their functions is gone through. There is a saltcellar of state, so called, and there may be a castor of state. How they use the salt, precisely—who knows? Certain I am, however, that a king’s head is solemnly oiled at his coronation, even as a head of salad. Can it be, though, that they anoint it with a view of making its interior run well, as they anoint machinery? Much might be ruminated here, concerning the essential dignity of this regal process, because in common life we esteem but meanly and contemptibly a fellow who anoints his hair, and palpably smells of that anointing. In truth, a mature man who uses hair-oil, unless medicinally, that man has probably got a quoggy spot in him somewhere. As a general rule, he can’t amount to much in his totality.

But the only thing to be considered here, is this—what kind of oil is used at coronations? Certainly it cannot be olive oil, nor macassar oil, nor castor oil, nor bear’s oil, nor train oil, nor cod-liver oil. What then can it possibly be, but sperm oil in its unmanufactured, unpolluted state, the sweetest of all oils?
Think of that, ye loyal Britons! we whalemen supply your kings and queens with coronation stuff!

modern_en.title: Chapter 25 — Postscript
paragraphs: In defense of the dignity of whaling, I would prefer to offer nothing but proven facts. But after marshaling his facts, an advocate who entirely suppressed a not unreasonable guess that might speak eloquently for his cause — would such an advocate not be to blame?

It is well known that at the coronation of kings and queens, even modern ones, a certain curious process of seasoning them for their duties is gone through. There is a so-called salt cellar of state, and there may be a castor of state, a ceremonial cruet. How exactly they use the salt — who knows? What I am certain of, however, is that a king's head is solemnly oiled at his coronation, just like a head of salad. Could it be, though, that they anoint it so that its interior will run well, the way one oils machinery? Much could be pondered here about the essential dignity of this royal process, because in ordinary life we think meanly and contemptuously of a fellow who oils his hair and plainly smells of it. In truth, a grown man who uses hair oil, unless for medical reasons, probably has a boggy spot in him somewhere. As a general rule, he can't amount to much taken as a whole.

But the only question to consider here is this: what kind of oil is used at coronations? It certainly can't be olive oil, or macassar oil, or castor oil, or bear's oil, or train oil, or cod-liver oil. What then can it possibly be, but sperm oil in its unprocessed, unpolluted state — the sweetest of all oils?
Think about that, you loyal Britons! We whalemen supply your kings and queens with their coronation stuff!

modern_da.title: Kapitel 25 — Efterskrift
paragraphs: Til forsvar for hvalfangstens værdighed ville jeg helst fremføre alene bevislige kendsgerninger. Men hvis en advokat, efter at have opstillet sine kendsgerninger, helt fortiede et ikke urimeligt gæt, som kunne tale veltalende for hans sag — ville en sådan advokat så ikke have skylden?

Det er velkendt, at man ved kroningen af konger og dronninger, selv moderne, gennemgår en vis besynderlig proces for at krydre dem til deres pligter. Der er et såkaldt statens saltkar, og der er måske en statens oliekande, en ceremoniel olieflaske. Hvordan de præcis bruger saltet — hvem ved? Men det er jeg sikker på, at en konges hoved højtideligt salves med olie ved hans kroning, ligesom et hoved salat. Men kunne det mon være, at de salver det, for at hans indre skal løbe godt, sådan som man olier maskineri? Der er meget at gruble over her angående denne kongelige handlings væsentlige værdighed, for i det almindelige liv tænker vi ringe og foragtelig om en mand, der olier sit hår og tydeligt lugter deraf. Sandt at sige har en voksen mand, der bruger hårolie, medmindre det er af helbredsgrunde, sandsynligvis et sumpet sted et eller andet sted i sig. Som en almindelig regel kan han ikke blive til meget, når man tager ham som helhed.

Men det eneste spørgsmål, der er værd at overveje her, er dette: Hvilken slags olie bruges ved kroninger? Det kan umuligt være olivenolie eller makassarolie eller ricinusolie eller bjørnefedt eller tran eller levertran. Hvad kan det så overhovedet være andet end spermolie i sin uforarbejdede, uforurenede tilstand — den sødeste af alle olier?
Tænk over det, I loyale briter! Vi hvalfangere leverer jeres konger og dronninger deres kroningsstof!
